title: How hard is it to find a job in Ireland right now?
excerpt: Unemployment is still low, but more people are competing for each job. Here is what the latest figures mean for jobseekers in Cork and across Ireland.
content_html:
Finding work in Ireland is still possible, but for many jobseekers it takes longer and needs more effort than it did a year or two ago. Here is what the latest figures show, and what they mean for you.

What the official figures say

The Central Statistics Office (CSO) reported that 149,500 people were unemployed in September 2026. The seasonally adjusted rate was 5%, and there were about 5,800 more unemployed people than a year earlier. The overall picture is steady rather than improving quickly.

The rate for people aged 15 to 24 is much higher, at 12.5%. If you are young or starting out, expect more competition for entry-level roles.

What recruiters are seeing

Morgan McKinley's Q3 2026 Ireland employment monitor reports that professional job openings were broadly steady over the quarter, but 4.8% lower than a year earlier. Over the same year, the number of jobseekers rose by 51%. In plain terms, there are fewer openings for each person looking.

Recruiters also describe employers as cautious. Hiring takes longer, and some firms fill business-critical projects with contract staff rather than permanent hires.

What this means for you

  • Apply early. Popular roles can close quickly, so check your job alerts every day.
  • Widen your search. Try related job titles, nearby towns, and temporary or contract work as a way in.
  • Build a steady routine. Ten well-targeted applications each week will do more than forty generic ones.
  • Keep a simple tracker of every application, with the date, the employer, and the contact name. Follow up about a week later.

The short answer

It is harder than it was, mostly because more people are looking for work, not because the jobs have disappeared. Candidates who stand out with a clear, tailored application get the interviews. The next posts in this series cover how to do that, including how to use AI tools safely.

Sources: Central Statistics Office, Monthly Unemployment, September 2026; Morgan McKinley, Ireland Employment Monitor Q3 2026.

title: How to use AI to find jobs online (and stay safe)
excerpt: AI tools can help you tailor your CV, research employers and practise interviews. Here is how to use them well, and how to avoid job scams while you do.
content_html:
AI assistants can save you a lot of time in a job search, as long as you stay in control of what they produce. Here are five practical ways to use them, followed by the safety rules that matter most.

1. Tailor your CV to each job

Paste the job advert and your current CV into an AI assistant and ask it which of your existing skills match the advert's wording. Then make the changes yourself. Check every suggestion, and keep only what is true. An AI tool should never invent experience, qualifications or dates.

2. Research the employer

Ask the assistant to summarise the employer's website, recent news and public reviews, and to suggest three questions to ask at interview. Then check the key facts on the employer's own site, because AI tools can be out of date or simply wrong.

3. Practise interviews

Ask for likely interview questions for the specific role, answer them out loud, and then ask for honest feedback on your answers. Practise with the questions in the advert, since those are the ones the interviewer is most likely to ask.

4. Draft cover notes faster

Give the assistant three points: why you want this job, your two strongest achievements, and the role's main requirements. Edit the draft until it sounds like you. Employers notice generic letters quickly.

5. Set up job alerts

Most major job boards let you save a search and receive email alerts. Set one up for each job title you want, and include a location. Alerts save you from refreshing the same pages every day.

Protect your personal information

Do not paste your PPS number, bank details, date of birth or ID numbers into an AI tool. Only share these through an employer's official application or onboarding process, and only once you are sure the employer is genuine.

Watch for job scams

Scams are common online, and AI has made fake adverts look more convincing. Be cautious if:

  • You are asked to pay for an application, training or equipment before you start work.
  • You are asked for bank details or your PPS number before a proper interview.
  • The job is offered through a messaging app, with no company name or website.
  • You are asked to receive and forward money or parcels for someone else.

If you are unsure, find the employer's website yourself rather than using the link in the message, and phone them directly using the number on their official site.

title: How to stand out from other candidates in Ireland
excerpt: When there are more applicants for each job, a clear and specific application makes the difference. Practical steps for your CV, cover note and interview.
content_html:
When a recruiter has dozens of applications to read, most of them are quickly dismissed. The good news is that a few simple changes can make your application much easier to shortlist.

Start with the job advert

Highlight the five to seven skills the employer asks for. Make sure your CV uses the same words for skills you genuinely have. Recruiters often search CVs for these exact terms.

Show results, not duties

Compare these two lines:

  • Responsible for stock in a busy shop.
  • Managed weekly stock orders for a busy shop, which reduced waste by 15% over six months.

The second line shows what you did and what changed. Only use figures you can back up in an interview.

Make the first page count

Recruiters scan CVs quickly. Put your most relevant experience and skills near the top, keep the CV to two pages, and use one clear font and simple headings. Leave out a photo, date of birth and marital status, which are not normally expected in Ireland.

Prove your skills with certificates

Certificates can move you up a shortlist, especially when they are a requirement. Common examples in Ireland include:

  • Safe Pass, for construction sites
  • Manual handling training, for warehouse, care and retail roles
  • Food safety or food hygiene certificates, for hospitality and food work
  • Driver CPC, for professional drivers
  • Garda vetting, which is needed for some care and childcare roles

Check which certificates the job asks for, and list the ones you have near the top of your CV with their dates.

Write a short, specific cover note

Use three short paragraphs. Say why you want to work for this employer, give one or two concrete examples of what you bring, and explain what you would like to do in the role. Do not repeat your CV word for word.

Prepare for the interview

Research the company, and prepare two or three examples from your experience using the STAR method: the Situation, the Task, the Action you took and the Result. Ask two or three thoughtful questions at the end, such as what a successful first three months looks like.

Follow up

Send a short thank-you email within a day of the interview. If you have not heard back by the date the employer gave, a polite follow-up email is fine. Keep it brief and professional.

title: The Irish CV: format, length and what to leave out
excerpt: Irish employers expect a clear, concise CV. Here is what to include, what to leave out, and how to make it easy to read in under a minute.
content_html:
Irish recruiters usually want a CV that is clear and easy to scan. There is no single required format, but these guidelines will serve you well for most roles.

Length

Two pages is the usual maximum for most jobseekers. Graduates and early-career candidates can often fit everything on one page. Cut anything that is not relevant to the job you are applying for.

What to include

  • Your name and contact details: a mobile number and a professional email address.
  • A short profile of two or three lines, describing the role you want and your strongest skills.
  • Work experience, most recent first, with dates, job titles and achievements.
  • Education and qualifications, including certificates and licences.
  • Relevant skills, such as languages, software or driving licence details.
  • A line on your right to work in Ireland, if it is relevant to the job.

What to leave out

  • A photo, date of birth, marital status or religion. These are not normally expected.
  • References listed by name. Write "References available on request" or simply leave it out.
  • Old or unrelated jobs that take up space. A part-time job from ten years ago does not need detail.
  • Spelling and grammar mistakes. Ask someone else to read the CV before you send it.

Make it easy to read

Use a standard font such as Arial or Calibri at 10 to 12 point, with clear headings and bullet points. Save the file with your name in the title, for example Mary-Murphy-CV.pdf, and send it as a PDF unless the employer asks for a Word file.

Finally, check that the CV matches what you say on LinkedIn and any online application form. Recruiters notice when the details do not agree.

title: Finding work in Cork beyond the job boards
excerpt: Many jobs are filled through networks, local services and direct contact with employers. Here are practical ways to widen your search in Cork.
content_html:
Online job boards are a good starting point, but they are not the only route to work. Many employers fill roles through referrals, local services or by contacting people they already know. Here are some ways to widen your search.

Use the free public employment services

Intreo centres, run by the Department of Social Protection, offer employment support, including help with CVs and interview preparation. The Local Employment Service (LES) also helps people find work in their local area. If you are receiving a jobseeker's payment, your Intreo officer can tell you what support is available.

Check training and apprenticeships

Further education courses and apprenticeships can lead directly to work. SOLAS and the education and training boards publish current courses and apprenticeships, many of them with employers involved. A short certified course can also make you more competitive for the jobs you are targeting.

Speak to employers directly

Choose five employers in Cork that you would like to work for. Visit their websites, look for their careers page, and send a short, polite email to the manager or team lead explaining what you can offer. Many small and medium-sized businesses never advertise their vacancies publicly.

Build your network

Tell friends, family, former colleagues and neighbours what kind of work you are looking for. Ask them to let you know about openings. Keep your LinkedIn profile up to date, and connect with people who work in the sectors you want to enter.

Watch for local events

Job fairs, employer open days and careers talks are often advertised on community boards, local libraries and social media. Attending even one can help you meet people who are hiring.

Keep a steady rhythm

Set aside time each week for your search, including applications, networking and follow-ups. A regular routine is easier to sustain than occasional bursts of effort, and it keeps you moving forward when responses are slow.
